interactions.label: In the DRSABC primary assessment, why is the airway checked before circulation?

params.question: In the DRSABC primary assessment, why is the airway checked before circulation?

answers.text: Airway obstruction can usually be corrected without any equipment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While basic airway manoeuvres are equipment-free, that is not why Airway precedes Circulation. The ordering is based on how quickly each problem kills.

answers.text: A blocked airway causes death faster than circulatory failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A blocked airway kills within minutes — faster than circulatory failure. Each step in DRSABC is sequenced by lethality speed, so the most time-critical threat is addressed first.

answers.text: Circulation cannot be accurately assessed until the airway is patent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Circulatory signs such as a radial pulse can be checked independently of airway patency. The ordering is driven by how fast each problem kills, not by assessment dependency.

answers.text: Assessing circulation requires an automated external defibrillator

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An AED assists with cardiac rhythm analysis, but circulation can be assessed by palpating a pulse or checking capillary refill. The sequence reflects lethality speed, not equipment requirements.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the reasoning: the DRSABC sequence prioritises threats by how quickly they cause death. A blocked airway kills in minutes — faster than absent circulation — so Airway is checked before Circulation.
Exactly right. DRSABC is ordered by how rapidly each threat kills: airway obstruction is the fastest, breathing failure next, and circulatory failure after that.

params.question: You find an adult collapsed and unresponsive on the pavement. After opening the airway, you observe slow, irregular, snoring gasps. What should you do immediately?

answers.text: Place the casualty in the recovery position and monitor breathing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The recovery position is for casualties who are breathing normally. Agonal gasps signal cardiac arrest, not effective ventilation — this casualty needs compressions, not monitoring.

answers.text: Begin chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Agonal gasps are slow, irregular breaths that appear just after cardiac arrest. They are NOT normal breathing. Begin compressions immediately — 5 to 6 cm deep, at 100 to 120 per minute, in cycles of 30 compressions to 2 breaths.

answers.text: Deliver two rescue breaths first, then check for a pulse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In the C-A-B sequence, compressions come first. The BLS protocol requires starting compressions without delay when the casualty is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

answers.text: Observe for ten more seconds to confirm the breathing pattern

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: You have already identified agonal gasps — further observation wastes time that could save a life. Every minute of delay in cardiac arrest reduces survival. Begin compressions immediately.

overallFeedback.feedback: Agonal gasps (slow, irregular, snoring breaths) signal cardiac arrest, not normal breathing. When a casualty is unresponsive with agonal gasps, begin chest compressions immediately at 100–120 per minute.
Well done. Recognising agonal gasps as a sign of cardiac arrest — not normal breathing — and starting compressions without delay is one of the most important BLS skills.

params.question: Once a triage category is assigned during a mass casualty incident, it remains unchanged throughout the response.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: That is incorrect. Triage is a dynamic, ongoing process. A casualty's condition can change — a 'delayed' (yellow) patient may deteriorate and need re-categorisation as 'immediate' (red). Triage must be repeated as the situation develops.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — triage is not a one-time verdict. A casualty's condition can improve or deteriorate as the situation evolves, so their triage category must be reassessed repeatedly throughout the response.

params.question: At a mass casualty scene, you are performing START triage. A casualty cannot walk, is breathing at 22 breaths per minute, has a palpable radial pulse, but does not follow your simple verbal command. What colour tag do you assign?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Green is only for the walking wounded. This casualty cannot walk and has failed the mental status check, ruling out a minor classification.

Yellow (delayed) requires the casualty to pass ALL three RPM parameters: respiratory rate under 30, adequate perfusion, AND the ability to follow commands. This casualty failed the mental status check.

Correct. In START triage, failure at any RPM checkpoint results in a red tag. This casualty's respiration (22/min) and perfusion (radial pulse present) are adequate, but inability to obey a simple command indicates compromised mental status — warranting an immediate (red) tag.
Black is assigned only when the casualty does not breathe even after the airway is opened. This casualty is breathing at 22 breaths per minute.

overallFeedback.feedback: Trace through the START algorithm: Respiration rate 22 (under 30 — pass), Perfusion with radial pulse (pass), Mental status cannot follow commands (fail). Any single RPM failure results in a red (immediate) tag.
Exactly right. In START triage, any RPM failure means a red tag. Remember the clinical pearl: the quiet, unresponsive casualties are often your sickest patients.
